articles.title: Why everyone’s switching to AI credits
articles.author: Kyle Poyar
articles.access_notes: Read via the publisher's legacy Substack archive (kylepoyar.substack.com/p/ai-credit-pricing); the canonical beehiiv site growthunhinged.com returned a Cloudflare bot-verification page to every fetch (WebFetch 403, curl 403, browser pane stuck on 'Performing security verification'), which was not bypassed. Substack marks the post subscriber-only; the public preview shows roughly the first third (about 660 of 1,881 words incl. a sponsor block). Text stops at the heading on what credits mean in practice; implementation guidance after that was not visible. Sponsor: Metronome (usage-billing vendor).
sections_read: Why everyone’s switching to AI credits

findings.summary: Large software vendors (Microsoft, Salesforce, Cursor, OpenAI and many SaaS firms) moved AI features to credit-based pricing during 2025; Kyle argues incumbents adopting it makes credits an accepted way to buy AI, easing adoption for smaller vendors.
findings.limitations: Vendor list and timing are as of Sep 2025; adoption by incumbents is not evidence that buyers prefer credits. Cursor's switch drew user pushback, which the author notes.

findings.summary: The main barrier to credits is buyer acceptance: credits can feel unpredictable, hard to manage and opaque, and procurement fears runaway cost without visibility.
findings.limitations: Opinion; no buyer data shown in the readable portion.

findings.summary: Kyle reports, from his own experience, that 70–80% of AI token consumption comes from about 10% of users, and that such heavy users become unprofitable without guardrails.
findings.section: Why everyone’s switching to AI credits
findings.limitations: Practitioner observation, no sample or method given; grade D for ClimbOS base rates. Concentration will vary by product.

findings.summary: Frontier model prices are not falling as fast as many predicted (newest models stay expensive while usage grows), so pricing that assumes costs will collapse soon, such as unlimited plans run at thin or negative margin, is risky.
findings.section: Why everyone’s switching to AI credits
findings.limitations: Cites a specific model token price as of Aug–Sep 2025; provider prices change often.

findings.summary: Credits suit this environment: buyers see a simple usage pool, while the vendor can re-rate actions as costs and value change, price newer high-value actions higher, include some free usage in existing or free plans, and let customers choose how to spend the pool.
findings.section: Why everyone’s switching to AI credits
findings.limitations: Benefits are asserted; the post's practical section (not visible) may add caveats.

articles.title: Your pricing is (probably) broken
articles.author: Kyle Poyar
articles.access_notes: Read via the publisher's legacy Substack archive (kylepoyar.substack.com/p/your-pricing-is-broken); the canonical beehiiv site growthunhinged.com returned a Cloudflare bot-verification page to every fetch (WebFetch 403, curl 403, browser pane stuck on 'Performing security verification'), which was not bypassed. Subscriber-only on Substack; preview showed the intro and the first three pricing models (about 970 of 1,747 words incl. sponsor). Later sections, presumably on usage, credit and outcome models, were not visible. Sponsor: Metronome.

findings.summary: No pricing model is perfect; the author advises making the most of the current model with targeted fixes rather than chasing newer models such as credits or outcome pricing out of embarrassment.
findings.limitations: Based on conversations with about three dozen software founders; anecdotal.

findings.summary: Flat-fee or unlimited plans are what customers ask for, but they price out small buyers, undercharge large ones, give no expansion path and allow low or negative margin customers. The fix is to add at least two expansion levers.
findings.limitations: Software-company framing; applies loosely to service retainers.

findings.summary: Kyle's rules of thumb: a premium edition priced 50–100% above base typically sees 15–25% uptake (he equates this to roughly +15% revenue); add-ons usually price at 10–30% of the core product; he cites his own earlier writing that about 1 in 3 B2B contracts include automatic renewal price increases, usually 5–8% a year; lite seats price at 10–40% of a full seat.
findings.limitations: Experience-based ranges from B2B software, no sample stated; escalator figure is self-cited from 2024. Treat as grade C/D priors, not targets.

findings.summary: Good-Better-Best tiers fail when plans feel arbitrary and most buyers default to the middle. Remedies: state each plan's purpose in one sentence; launch one or two new features a year as add-ons and fold them into higher tiers roughly every 18 months; consider progressive feature gating that gives every plan a taste of premium features.
findings.limitations: Cadence numbers are the author's heuristic.

findings.summary: Seats remain common but weaken as AI reduces headcount and agent value does not scale with logins. Rather than abandoning seats, redefine them: lite seats, minimum seat counts on team plans, usage limits by plan, or pilot usage pricing for select large customers using their past usage as a baseline.
findings.limitations: Examples are large software vendors; small businesses rarely sell seats.

articles.title: A new framework for AI agent pricing
articles.author: Manny Medina (guest; intro by Kyle Poyar)
articles.access_notes: Read via the publisher's legacy Substack archive (kylepoyar.substack.com/p/ai-agent-pricing-framework); the canonical beehiiv site growthunhinged.com returned a Cloudflare bot-verification page to every fetch (WebFetch 403, curl 403, browser pane stuck on 'Performing security verification'), which was not bypassed. Public (everyone) on the Substack archive; full text read. Diagrams/graphics were images and not read. Author is founder of Paid, a billing platform for results-based AI agent pricing: commercial interest in the outcome model he favours.
sections_read: The four AI Agent pricing models dominating the market
Decision framework: Choosing the right pricing model for your AI agent

findings.summary: Of 175 signups to Paid at launch, 130 (about 75%) said they were unsure how to price AI features.
findings.limitations: Self-selected signups to a pricing-tool vendor, early 2025; shows uncertainty among that audience only.

findings.summary: Four agent pricing models: per agent (a fixed fee positioned against a hire), per action (consumption, often tokens or minutes plus margin), per workflow (a completed multi-step process), and per outcome (pay only for a defined result). Hybrids with seats are common.
findings.section: The four AI Agent pricing models
findings.limitations: Based on the author's review of 60+ AI agent companies; method not described.

findings.summary: Trade-offs: per-agent is predictable and draws on headcount budgets but invites 'same but cheaper' rivals; per-action is transparent but commoditises and tracks falling costs down; per-workflow balances the two but long or complex runs can go margin-negative; per-outcome aligns best with value but needs predictable performance, clear success definitions and attribution, and can lead to bespoke contracts.
findings.limitations: Claims about budget size (headcount budget 'at least 10x' tools budget) are unsourced assertions.

findings.summary: Decision questions: is the agent replacing a defined headcount (per agent, or time saved × hourly rate for workflows); can the outcome be measured and attributed reliably (per outcome, or outcome bonuses on another model); are tasks varied with unpredictable volume (per action, possibly with a per-agent base).
findings.limitations: Framework is qualitative; no tested thresholds.

findings.summary: The author predicts core model costs will fall 10–100x over 3–5 years, pressuring per-action pricing most, and believes outcome pricing will win long term.
findings.limitations: Forecast plus vendor interest (Paid sells outcome billing). GU-01 notes newest-model prices had not fallen as expected by late 2025.

articles.title: The state of SaaS pricing
articles.author: Kyle Poyar
articles.access_notes: Read via the publisher's legacy Substack archive (kylepoyar.substack.com/p/the-state-of-usage-based-pricing); the canonical beehiiv site growthunhinged.com returned a Cloudflare bot-verification page to every fetch (WebFetch 403, curl 403, browser pane stuck on 'Performing security verification'), which was not bypassed. Subscriber-only on Substack; preview showed about 1,200 of 2,252 words, through the seven hybrid examples. The body of 'Common pitfalls of usage-based pricing' was not visible. Slug says usage-based pricing; displayed title is 'The state of SaaS pricing'.
sections_read: It’s no longer usage-based pricing vs. subscriptions

Seven hybrid examples (usage-based expansion; usage-based subscriptions; transaction revenue + subscriptions; success-based; usage pricing for specific segments; active-user subscriptions; credit-based ELAs)
Common pitfalls of usage-based pricing (heading only)

findings.summary: In a survey of private SaaS companies Kyle cites (over 3,000 respondents across six annual surveys, 700+ in 2023, fielded in Q3), usage-based pricing adoption fell from 46% to 41% year on year, with 17% testing it.
findings.limitations: SaaS-only, venture-oriented respondents, 2022–2023; self-reported; not small local businesses.

findings.summary: Most usage-based businesses in that survey use a hybrid of subscription plus usage rather than pure pay-as-you-go, especially those selling to smaller customers who are more sensitive to unplanned bills.
findings.limitations: Same survey caveats; the readable text gives the direction, not the exact split.

findings.summary: The real contrast is not usage vs subscription but flexible, consumption-linked pricing vs rigid upfront commitments tied to access. Hybrid patterns include: usage included in plans with paid overage; plans stepped by usage allowance; subscription plus transaction fees; success fees as an add-on; pay-as-you-go for occasional users; charging only for active users; and committed spend drawn down flexibly.
findings.section: It’s no longer usage-based pricing vs. subscriptions
findings.limitations: Examples are large software vendors (as of early 2024); their specific prices are dated.

findings.summary: Usage pricing is more than a price change: it touches billing, forecasting, sales compensation and organisation, and usage businesses saw faster revenue deceleration in the 2022–2023 slowdown.
findings.limitations: Deceleration claim is stated without the underlying data in the readable part.

articles.title: Your guide to SaaS packaging 201
articles.author: Kyle Poyar
articles.access_notes: Read via the publisher's legacy Substack archive (kylepoyar.substack.com/p/your-guide-to-saas-packaging-201); the canonical beehiiv site growthunhinged.com returned a Cloudflare bot-verification page to every fetch (WebFetch 403, curl 403, browser pane stuck on 'Performing security verification'), which was not bypassed. Subscriber-only on Substack; preview covered the intro and the first two principles (about 750 of 1,717 words). Principle 3 onward was not visible.
sections_read: 1. Good-Better-Best is the de-facto starting point
2. Leave room for add-ons – but be selective about it
3. Each package needs a job in your revenue generation (heading only)

findings.summary: Kyle states that about two-thirds of SaaS companies use a three-tier Good-Better-Best lineup.
findings.limitations: No source or sample given in the readable part; SaaS only.

findings.summary: Good-Better-Best sits between a single inflexible offer (no upsell) and build-your-own packaging (decision paralysis, nickel-and-diming, more line items to negotiate). It eases choice, segments by willingness to pay, creates an upsell path and funds new products. Default to it when unsure.
findings.limitations: Author notes his principles may conflict and not fit all contexts.

findings.summary: Sell a capability as an add-on when it is polarising (a few value it highly), serves a different buyer or budget, replaces spend on another vendor, is adopted much later than purchase, or carries real delivery cost you want only willing payers to use. Keep it to one or two add-ons at first purchase, each easy to explain.
findings.limitations: Heuristics from B2B software sales; not tested thresholds.

articles.title: Your guide to reverse trials
articles.author: Kyle Poyar (with Lauryn Isford, then Airtable)
articles.access_notes: Read via the publisher's legacy Substack archive (kylepoyar.substack.com/p/your-guide-to-reverse-trials); the canonical beehiiv site growthunhinged.com returned a Cloudflare bot-verification page to every fetch (WebFetch 403, curl 403, browser pane stuck on 'Performing security verification'), which was not bypassed. Subscriber-only on Substack; preview covered the freemium vs trial trade-offs and the reverse-trial definition (about 670 of 2,333 words). The Airtable interview answers were not visible.
sections_read: Inside Airtable’s reverse trial strategy (intro only)

findings.summary: Free-trial products see higher free-to-paid conversion than freemium, often 2–3x, while freemium sees higher visitor-to-signup conversion; Kyle links external sources for both.
findings.limitations: Linked sources were not read; 2022 PLG software data; the two rates use different denominators (trial starters vs free users).

findings.summary: Choose by trade-off: freemium favours acquisition, longer time-to-value and viral or network products; free trials favour conversion speed and cash payback. He illustrates median time to purchase as perhaps 14 days for trials vs 60–90 for freemium.
findings.limitations: Time-to-purchase figures are illustrative ('might be'), not measured.

findings.summary: A reverse trial starts new users on a time-limited trial of paid features, then they buy or drop to a permanent free tier, aiming to get both acquisition and conversion and to use loss aversion.
findings.limitations: Benefit claims rely on general behavioural findings; product-specific results unknown from the readable text.

articles.title: Customers don't care about your AI feature
articles.author: Kristen Berman (guest, Irrational Labs)
articles.access_notes: Read via the publisher's legacy Substack archive (kylepoyar.substack.com/p/ai-messaging-study); the canonical beehiiv site growthunhinged.com returned a Cloudflare bot-verification page to every fetch (WebFetch 403, curl 403, browser pane stuck on 'Performing security verification'), which was not bypassed. Public (everyone) on the Substack archive; full text read including the footnote correction. Charts were images; values taken from text only.
sections_read: The surprising science behind AI labels and what our research revealed
So why do companies still overuse “AI” in their marketing?
How you should market your AI feature (1–4)

findings.summary: In a controlled experiment with 767 US participants shown landing pages for four real products with or without explicit AI wording, labelling as 'generative AI' significantly lowered expected impact; willingness to pay differed by about $1, not statistically significant; trust was largely unchanged. One product was an exception.
findings.section: The surprising science behind AI labels
findings.limitations: Online panel, mostly mainstream users (68% had used AI a few times, 15% daily); not early adopters; stated WTP, not purchases; four products; period late 2024/early 2025; consultancy author.

findings.summary: Market AI features by the result: plain-language benefits, specific measured gains (time or money saved), letting users try a feature before it becomes paid (endowment, reverse trial), and when 'AI' must appear, pair it with a clear use case or a benefit-led name.
findings.section: How you should market your AI feature
findings.limitations: Recommendations extend beyond what the experiment tested; quoted vendor stats are those vendors' claims.

findings.summary: A behavioural redesign that framed a setup call as unlocking a device ('their' device) was reported alongside other changes to raise successful device pairing by 90% for a health-device company.
findings.limitations: Single consultancy case, combined interventions, no baseline given.

findings.summary: PricingSaaS reports 42% of companies in its index changed prices in the first three quarters of 2024; Kyle's intro says increases were the most common change, averaging about 20%.
findings.limitations: Vendor-run index of public SaaS pricing pages, Q1–Q3 2024; denominator ambiguous (443 vs 3,000+); list prices only, not realised prices.

findings.summary: Monday.com raised its most popular plan about 20% but its entry plan only 12.5% to keep the entry price under a $10 per-seat threshold, and justified the rise with a visible record of added features.

findings.summary: Pricing-page clarity matters: plan names should signal who each plan is for (e.g., not calling a top tier 'Plus'), defaults such as the pre-filled team size shape perceived price and target segment, and confusing ordering, mixed audiences on one grid or many badges hurt comprehension.

concepts.name: Credit allowance with heavy-user guardrails
concepts.decision: Whether to sell variable-cost work (AI generation, research, messages, jobs) as unlimited, pure pay-as-you-go, or a plan allowance in credits with top-ups, and how to rate each action so heavy users don't erase margin.
applies_when: Delivery cost per customer varies widely with use (AI calls, data lookups, sends, minutes)
Customers want a predictable bill but usage differs a lot between them
The business offers several actions with very different cost or value
avoid_when: Cost per customer is flat and low (credits add confusion for no margin benefit)
Buyers can't relate credits to anything they value and no estimator can be shown
No metering exists to count usage per customer
evidence_required: Per-customer variable cost for at least one full billing cycle
Share of total variable cost from the top 10% of customers
Cost per action type, versioned by date
Customer comprehension check of the credit unit (can they predict their bill?)
prerequisites: Usage metering per customer and action
Billing that supports allowances and top-ups
steps: Compute cost per customer per month; rank customers; record the top-decile cost share
List actions; set credit rates by value to the buyer, with a floor of cost / (1 − target margin)
Size each plan's allowance so a customer who uses it all still meets the margin floor
Offer clearly priced top-ups or a fair-use limit for the heavy tail rather than raising everyone's price
Show the credit cost before any expensive action and a balance meter; never auto-charge overage without consent
Re-rate actions when provider costs or value change, with notice
alternatives: No metering: use a fair-use cap on the top plan and review manually monthly
Low volume: one plan plus a single paid add-on for the costly action
Small budget/no billing integration: sell prepaid packs by invoice
Missing cost data: use provider invoices ÷ active customers as an average and flag distribution as unknown
metrics: Contribution margin per customer (distribution, not just average)
Share of customers hitting allowance; top-up attach rate
Breakage (unused credits) tracked separately from earned margin
guardrails: Fully used allowance meets the margin floor; breakage is never the plan that makes the margin
No hidden overage; balance and per-action cost visible
Re-rating applies only with advance notice; purchased credits keep their stated value
Do not degrade the core promised outcome to save cost
concepts.observation_window: Two full billing cycles after launch or re-rating; heavy-user share reviewed monthly.
stop_review: Top-decile customers are contribution-negative after two cycles: re-rate or cap
Surprise-bill tickets or refunds rise: simplify the unit or add an estimator
Conversion drops versus the prior flat plan with no margin gain: revert
concepts.climbos_location: Plan engine (offer/economics diagnosis), PB-pricing-test variant, margin calculator, pricing page advice. Separately: ClimbOS's own credit pricing review (see GU.md arithmetic).

inputs_hypothetical.business: Booking app for salons with AI reply drafting

expected_behavior: Notes 70% average margin hides ten customers at about -$50 contribution each
Proposes an allowance whose full use costs at most $28 plus priced top-ups or a fair-use cap for the heavy tail
Asks for comprehension testing and a balance display
Labels the 70–80%/10% concentration figure as the author's experience, not a benchmark
hard_failure: Raising price for all customers as the only fix
Recommending unlimited usage on the strength of expected falling AI costs

concepts.interpretation: Interpretation: Kyle's case for credits is mainly about cost concentration and the vendor's freedom to re-rate actions; buyer predictability is the cost. For small businesses the same logic applies to any capped package of variable work (e.g., included revisions, call minutes).
concepts.proposed_rule: Proposed ClimbOS rule: when a customer's variable cost per account varies by more than a set ratio, the engine checks the top-decile cost share and the margin of a fully used allowance before recommending flat or unlimited pricing; recommendations must pass the margin floor at full allowance use, excluding breakage.
concepts.overlaps_existing: Extends guides/02_monetization.md (heavy-use scenario, allowance + top-up hypothesis) and growth-intelligence book 12 §10–11 (distribution over average, reserve cost before expensive work). Adds the concentration metric, re-rating, and the breakage rule. Versions PB-pricing-test with a credit/allowance variant.
concepts.disagreements: Book 12 warns usage pricing needs clear metering and understanding; GU-01 claims credits feel simple to buyers. Decide by a comprehension test: if owners cannot predict their monthly credit use within a reasonable band, prefer plan tiers with a fair-use cap. GU-03 predicts 10–100x cost falls; GU-01 says newest-model costs had not fallen by late 2025. Rule: price on current observed cost, never on forecast declines.

concepts.name: Charging-model eligibility gates (seat, flat, usage-hybrid, workflow, outcome)
concepts.decision: Which billing unit fits a business whose product does work for the customer: per person, flat subscription, usage allowance, per completed job/workflow, or per result.
applies_when: Owner is choosing or changing what they charge per (not just how much)
The product or service automates work previously done by staff or contractors
Owner is drawn to outcome or success pricing
avoid_when: Pricing is set by a dominant marketplace or regulation
Fewer than a handful of customers and no delivery history (start with a simple fixed offer and learn)
evidence_required: Can the outcome be defined, measured and attributed to the business without dispute?
Variance of delivery cost per job
Customer's current alternative and its cost (staff time, agency, contractor)
Customer's need for bill predictability
Cash buffer to carry delivery cost before outcome fees are paid
prerequisites: Written outcome definition and attribution method if outcome pricing is considered
steps: Describe what the customer values and how they measure it
Gate outcome pricing: measurable + attributable + performance predictable + cash can carry the lag; otherwise drop to workflow or job pricing, or add an outcome bonus on a base fee
Gate per-job/workflow pricing: jobs are standard enough to price; cap or surcharge long-running jobs
Gate usage pricing: volume varies a lot between customers; for small buyers prefer a hybrid (base plan + allowance) over pure pay-as-you-go
Gate replacement framing (price against a hire): the offer covers a defined role's typical output; price as a share of that cost and expect cheaper copycats
Compare two or three candidate models with the owner's own numbers before any price-point optimisation
alternatives: Attribution unclear: base fee + capped success bonus
Low volume: fixed-scope package per job
No tracking integration: monthly retainer with a stated volume ceiling
metrics: Contribution per job and per customer
Days from delivery cost to cash received
Win rate and churn by model
guardrails: Outcome definitions written before work starts; no retroactive redefinition
No outcome pricing in regulated categories where contingent fees are restricted without owner/legal review
Show total expected cost range to the buyer
concepts.observation_window: One full sales cycle plus one delivery cycle per model tried; outcome models need at least the attribution window plus payment terms.
stop_review: Disputes over outcomes exceed an agreed share: move to base + bonus
Workflow jobs run margin-negative repeatedly: add caps or re-scope
Buyers stall on unpredictability: add a base plan or ceiling
concepts.climbos_location: Plan engine offer/economics stage and Climb AI pricing questions; owner-input form fields (outcome measurability, attribution, cash buffer); new contract field for PB-pricing-test 'billing unit' changes.

inputs_hypothetical.business: Two-person lead-gen agency for local contractors
inputs_hypothetical.attribution: appointments booked through client's own phone line, not tracked

expected_behavior: Flags that attribution is not reliable and cash buffer is thin
Recommends base retainer plus a per-appointment bonus with call tracking, or a fixed package until tracking exists
States the outcome model's preconditions explicitly
hard_failure: Endorsing pure pay-per-result without an attribution method
Citing the guest author's 'outcome pricing will win' as evidence for this business

concepts.interpretation: Interpretation: GU-03's four models map to small-business terms as retainer-per-role, pay-as-you-go, per-job and success fee. The durable content is the gating conditions, not the forecast.
concepts.proposed_rule: Proposed ClimbOS rule: the engine may recommend outcome or success pricing only when the owner confirms a written outcome definition, an attribution method and cash to carry delivery cost; otherwise it offers base + bonus or per-job pricing and explains which gate failed.
concepts.overlaps_existing: Extends guides/02_monetization.md ('compare charging models before optimizing a price point') and book 12 §10 with explicit eligibility gates. Complements BK02 Ch 8 strategy-type eligibility (penetration/skimming/maximisation), which covers price level, not billing unit.
concepts.disagreements: GU-03 (vendor of outcome billing) says outcome pricing wins long term; GU-02 says no model is perfect and to optimise the current one. For small businesses ClimbOS sides with GU-02 by default; outcome pricing only when the gates pass. GU-04's survey shows small-customer sellers prefer hybrids, consistent with 02_monetization's predictability concern.

concepts.name: Package architecture and expansion levers
concepts.decision: How to structure tiers and add-ons, and which lever to add when a single flat offer leaves no room for customers to pay more as they get more value.
applies_when: One flat price for everyone, little or no expansion revenue
Best customers clearly get more value than others
A new capability is launching and the owner asks whether to include it or charge for it
avoid_when: Customer count too small to tell segments apart (start with one offer plus one add-on)
Tier differences would gate something the entry plan needs to deliver its promise
Operating more packages would overload support or billing
evidence_required: Segments with different jobs or willingness to pay (interviews, purchase data)
Which features or services customers name as the reason they buy
Adoption timing of features after purchase
Cost to deliver each capability
steps: Write one sentence per plan: who it is for and why they buy
Default to three tiers when segments differ; one offer when they don't
Run the add-on test for each capability: polarising, different buyer/budget, replaces another vendor, adopted later, or costly to serve
Limit first purchase to one or two add-ons
Pick one expansion lever to test: premium tier, paid add-on, usage limit by tier, lite access level, minimum team size, or a disclosed annual escalator on new contracts
Fold proven add-ons into a higher tier periodically to keep the lineup simple
alternatives: Low traffic: offer the premium option in sales conversations and log acceptance before publishing
Service business: premium = faster turnaround or priority access; add-on = optional extra service
No billing integration: separate invoice line items
metrics: Revenue per customer and contribution per customer
Downgrades and cannibalisation from top tier
guardrails: Entry plan must deliver its advertised outcome
No decoy-only tiers (BK02 rule)
Escalators disclosed at signup, applied only per contract terms
Existing customers' terms unchanged during tests (PB-pricing-test)
concepts.observation_window: At least one full renewal or repurchase cycle; 8–12 weeks of new signups for uptake reads, longer at low volume.
stop_review: Premium uptake well below plan and base conversion falls: rethink tier boundaries
Add-on causes billing confusion or complaints: bundle it
More than two add-ons routinely needed: repackage
concepts.climbos_location: Pricing page advice, plan engine offer stage, PB-pricing-test (versioned variant: 'add an expansion lever'), Climb AI packaging Q&A, revenue calculator.

inputs_hypothetical.observation: a third of clients ask for payroll and monthly calls

expected_behavior: Suggests payroll as an add-on (different need, costly to serve) or a premium tier with calls
Computes revenue lift as uptake × price difference using owner assumptions labelled hypothetical
Keeps base package delivering full bookkeeping
Labels the 15–25% uptake range as one author's software experience
hard_failure: Moving core bookkeeping into the premium tier
Promising Kyle's +15% revenue as an expected result

concepts.interpretation: Interpretation: the add-on test is the most transferable piece for small businesses; numeric uptake and pricing ratios are software heuristics to use only as starting assumptions.
concepts.proposed_rule: Proposed ClimbOS rule: every package recommendation states each plan's buyer and reason in one sentence, passes the add-on test for each extra, and shows expansion revenue as uptake × price difference with owner-supplied or clearly labelled assumed uptake.
concepts.overlaps_existing: Extends guides/02_monetization.md (coherent package boundaries) and BK02 review Ch 10/11 (benefit lines per plan, compromise tier, no decoys). New: add-on eligibility test, expansion-lever menu, rebundling cadence. Versions PB-pricing-test.
concepts.disagreements: BK02 Ch 11 treats a middle tier as a compromise-effect tactic; GU-02 warns everyone defaulting to the middle can be a symptom of arbitrary plans. Decide by plan-choice data: if most buyers choose the middle and the top tier sees near-zero uptake, revisit boundaries rather than adding anchors.

concepts.name: Free plan vs free trial vs reverse trial
concepts.decision: Which try-before-you-buy model to use for a self-serve product or a sampleable service, given acquisition, conversion speed and cash needs.
applies_when: Self-serve software, app or digital product
Service businesses considering a free first session or sample (by analogy)
Owner debating freemium vs trial, or conversion from free is low
avoid_when: High-touch sales where trials are run by hand anyway
Free usage carries material variable cost the business can't fund
Value can't be experienced within any trial length and there's no free tier option
evidence_required: Visitor-to-signup and signup-to-paid rates by model (owner data, or labelled fallbacks from base-rates.md)
Time to first value
Variable cost per free user
Cash runway or payback requirement
Whether value grows with more users (virality/network)
prerequisites: Product analytics for signup, first value and conversion
steps: Measure time to first value; if longer than a plausible trial, lean freemium or reverse trial
Estimate paid customers per 1,000 visitors for each model using owner data or labelled assumptions
Account for timing: trials convert sooner, which matters if cash funds acquisition
Consider a reverse trial: full features for a limited time, then a free tier
Test one model change for new signups only; compare paid per visitor, not paid per signup
alternatives: Low traffic: sequential before/after with whole-week cohorts and caveats
No gating ability: time-limited trial by account flag
Service business: paid first session at a discount instead of free
metrics: Retention of converted users by model
guardrails: Never compare trial and freemium conversion rates directly (different denominators)
Clear notice before a trial ends; no silent card charge
Downgrade keeps the user's data
concepts.observation_window: At least two full trial lengths plus a 30–60 day window for freemium conversions; whole weeks.
stop_review: Paid per visitor falls versus baseline after the window: revert
Free-user cost exceeds the agreed budget: tighten the free tier
Support load from downgrades spikes: improve messaging
concepts.climbos_location: Plan engine activation/conversion stage; PB-activation-repair (alternative branch); calculator for paid-per-visitor comparison; base-rates.md fallbacks.

expected_behavior: Compares models on paid per 1,000 visitors with labelled assumptions
Computes the reverse-trial conversion needed to beat each alternative
Recommends a test on new signups with a fixed window
Mentions faster cash from trials given short runway
hard_failure: Claiming a trial 'converts 2–3x better' without noting denominators
Declaring a winner from one week of data

concepts.interpretation: Interpretation: the useful decision variable is paid customers per visitor over a fixed window, with conversion timing as a cash factor; the reverse trial is a hedge when time-to-value is short but acquisition matters.
concepts.proposed_rule: Proposed ClimbOS rule: trial-model recommendations must compute paid per 1,000 visitors and days to cash for each candidate, and must never compare per-trial and per-free-user conversion directly.
concepts.overlaps_existing: Extends skills/growth-plays/reference/base-rates.md (free plan 2–5%, trial 15–25%, card-required 40–60%; grade C) with the denominator caveat and reverse-trial option; complements PB-activation-repair. No existing reverse-trial coverage found in docs/skills/shared.
concepts.disagreements: Base-rates implies a much larger gap (roughly 3–12x) between trial and free-plan conversion than GU-06's 2–3x. Not contradictory: different denominators and sources. Resolve by using owner data and per-visitor comparison.

concepts.name: Lead with the outcome, not the AI label
concepts.decision: How to describe and price an AI-enabled feature or service on landing and pricing pages.
applies_when: Owner adds AI to a product or service and wants to mention it or raise price because of it
Pricing page or ad copy leads with 'AI-powered'
avoid_when: Audience is explicitly early adopters or tech buyers seeking AI tools (findings may not apply)
Disclosure of AI use is required by law or platform policy (disclose, but still lead with benefit)
evidence_required: Measured outcome of the feature (time saved, errors reduced) from the owner's own users
Comprehension or preference check of copy variants where traffic allows
prerequisites: A way to measure the feature's effect (feature flag, before/after)
steps: Rewrite headline around the customer's result in plain language
Quantify the gain only with the owner's measured data
Let users try the feature before it becomes paid where cost allows
If 'AI' is used, pair it with a concrete use case
Justify any price change with delivered value, not the AI label
alternatives: No measurement yet: describe the task removed, without numbers
Low traffic: 5-second or comprehension test with a few customers
metrics: Upgrade rate to plan containing the feature
guardrails: No invented or borrowed performance stats
Required AI disclosures kept
No price increase justified solely by 'now with AI'
concepts.observation_window: Whole weeks until each variant has enough visitors for the agreed decision rule; otherwise qualitative test.
stop_review: Benefit-led copy underperforms the AI-led version with adequate sample: keep AI framing for this audience
concepts.climbos_location: Content/copy generation rules, pricing page advice, Climb AI copy review, landing-split playbook (PB-landing-split) hypothesis library.

inputs_hypothetical.plan: add 'AI-powered bookkeeping' and raise monthly fee 20%

expected_behavior: Advises leading with client outcome (e.g., faster month-end close) and measuring before claiming numbers
Says the AI label alone is unlikely to lift willingness to pay, citing the 767-person study with its caveats
Separates price decision from label
hard_failure: Writing 'AI-powered' headlines with invented time-saved figures
Endorsing the 20% rise on the AI label alone

concepts.interpretation: Interpretation: the study supports benefit-first copy for mainstream buyers; it does not show AI mentions harm early-adopter audiences.
concepts.proposed_rule: Proposed ClimbOS rule: generated copy leads with the customer outcome; 'AI' appears only as supporting detail unless the owner's audience is AI-seeking; no price justification rests on the AI label.
concepts.overlaps_existing: Extends BK02 review Ch 10 (benefits not features, no unproven advantages) with direct evidence on AI labels. Mentions of 'AI-powered' exist in docs/research/acquisition-framework.md and channel-content.md; check those for conflicting copy advice.
concepts.disagreements: None with BK02. Possible conflict with SEO/AEO advice that favours keyword-heavy 'AI' copy; resolve by keeping AI terms in supporting content and metadata while headlines lead with outcomes.

concepts.name: Segmented price increase with value proof
concepts.decision: Whether and how to raise list prices, especially on popular or unlimited plans, without losing price-sensitive customers.
applies_when: Prices unchanged while value or costs rose
Unlimited or flat top plan attracts heavy users
Owner considers a single large increase
avoid_when: Diagnosis points to weak value, delivery or communication (fix those first, BK02)
Existing contracts forbid changes before renewal
No record of added value to explain the change
evidence_required: Revenue and customer counts per plan
Variable cost per plan, incl. heavy users
Changelog of value added since last price change
Price thresholds relevant to the segment
Contract/notice terms for existing customers
prerequisites: Owner authorisation and a reviewed migration plan for existing customers
steps: Decide new-customer vs existing-customer scope separately
Raise most on the plan with the most demonstrated value; protect the entry price below a key threshold
For unlimited plans, prefer adjusting usage limits or adding a usage component over a very large jump
Compute the churn level at which revenue and contribution break even
Announce with the value record and adequate notice
Monitor churn and downgrades by plan against the break-even
alternatives: Low volume: apply to new customers first and observe
No cost data: raise on new customers only and add a fair-use clause
Thin evidence: small steps tied to product improvements (BK02 Ch 12)
metrics: Churn and downgrade rate vs break-even
guardrails: Existing customers get advance notice per terms; no silent changes
Not a pricing test (PB-pricing-test keeps existing terms unchanged)
No fake 'was' prices
concepts.observation_window: One renewal cycle for existing customers; 8–12 weeks of new signups.
stop_review: Churn exceeds the computed break-even: pause and review
Conversion of new customers falls sharply: reconsider level or packaging
concepts.climbos_location: New playbook candidate (PB-price-increase, proposed) beside PB-capacity, whose signature currently captures 'price increase' only as a capacity response; plan engine economics stage; calculator for break-even churn.

expected_behavior: Suggests a smaller entry increase that stays below a threshold and a larger core-plan increase if value supports it
Computes break-even churn
Separates new vs existing customers and requires notice
hard_failure: Applying the PricingSaaS 20% average as a recommended increase
Raising existing customers' prices without notice

concepts.interpretation: Interpretation: the cases show segmentation (protect entry price, raise the core plan, tie to value) and suggest limit changes beat large jumps on unlimited plans; no outcomes were reported, so these are patterns, not proof.
concepts.proposed_rule: Proposed ClimbOS rule: any price-increase recommendation shows per-plan increases, the break-even churn, scope (new vs existing), required notice and the value record; increases on unlimited plans first consider limit or usage changes.
concepts.overlaps_existing: Extends BK02 review (Ch 8 increase cadence; Ch 12 small steps tied to improvements) and PB-capacity (price increase as a capacity response). Fills the gap where 'price increase' routes only to delivery/capacity in shared/agents/diagnosis.ts.
concepts.disagreements: PB-pricing-test forbids changing existing customers' terms; a price increase is a separate, owner-authorised migration, not a test. 02_monetization requires a reviewed migration plan, consistent with this rule.
